entries.title: Graded Intersection Types
entries.abstract: We introduce graded intersection types, in which arrow domains are multisets of types with coefficients in a semiring. Boolean and natural number grades recover idempotent and non-idempotent intersection types. We give algebraic conditions on the semiring for subject reduction and expansion in finite systems and in locally finite systems with guarded infinite types. We construct a lifting to multisets of grades corresponding, in this general setting, to lifting the idempotent system to the non-idempotent one. We recall the main existing operational characterisations from the literature, and show some general extensions.

entries.title: Mathematical foundations for symmetric programming and reasoning
entries.abstract: We develop a mathematical abstraction for uniformly exploiting symmetries in programming and reasoning based on the mathematical proof principle `without-loss-of-generality' (w.l.o.g.). Given: group actions that describe symmetries of the input and the output; and a canoniser, which captures how arbitrary inputs get sent to canonical ones, our construction extends any function from the canonical inputs to the whole domain. We characterise the conditions on the canonisers which guarantee that the construction gives the unique equivariant (i.e. symmetry-preserving) extension. Furthermore, we adapt the construction to a dependently-typed setting, where it captures traditional symmetric w.l.o.g. arguments via the Curry-Howard correspondence. Finally, we extend the construction to algebraic data types, where the symmetries of the constructors both uniquely determine the symmetries of the data type and pave the way for efficient execution.

entries.title: AMARA: Compiler-Driven Accelerator Architecture Design for Graphical Probabilistic Sampling
entries.abstract: Sampling methods are fundamental primitives for training and inference on probabilistic models. However, practical deployment of sampling algorithms such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) remains difficult on general-purpose processors. Existing hardware accelerators improve sampling efficiency, but they are typically specialized for a narrow class of models, graph topologies, or update schedules, making it difficult to support the diverse workloads used in real applications. This paper presents AMARA, an end-to-end compiler-driven accelerator framework for probabilistic sampling on arbitrary probabilistic graphical models. AMARA introduces MCMC-IR, a domain-specific intermediate representation that separates local factorized computation from global update dependencies. Based on this representation, the compiler performs architecture-aware partitioning, scheduling, and memory-access optimization to expose parallelism and reduce irregular graph communication. The optimized program is lowered to a compact ISA and executed on a programmable ASIC accelerator with specialized compute, sampling, and memory support. By co-designing the compiler and the architecture, AMARA bridges the gap between model generality and accelerator efficiency for practical MCMC-based probabilistic computing. We evaluate AMARA across representative workloads with different structures, including grid-structured and irregular energy-based models, and causal inference networks. The results show that AMARA supports a broad spectrum of discrete probabilistic models while achieving high sampling throughput and efficient hardware utilization. AMARA achieves an average of 6.1× (up to 16.3×) higher sampling throughput than a JAX-GPU baseline on irregular workloads, and offers broader programmability than state-of-the-art accelerators.

entries.title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning
entries.abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in software engineering and have performed well on different programming tasks. However, it is still difficult to know whether these models truly understand program behavior or whether they mainly rely on patterns learned from their training data. This distinction is particularly important for intermediate representations (IRs), where operations, dataflow, and execution semantics are explicitly represented. In this paper, we introduce MLIRBench, a benchmark for evaluating how LLMs reason about MLIR programs. MLIRBench uses a multi-agent pipeline to generate program mutations, validate their behavior through execution, and construct reasoning tasks from torch and linalg program pairs. The dataset contains 1,768 validated pairs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs, labeled as EQUIV, DIVERGE, or ERROR. We evaluated nine models, including five open-weight and four proprietary models. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest hard-label accuracy of 92.65% across all 1,768 pairs, counting unsuccessful predictions as incorrect. Across its 1,768 scored predictions, it achieved an aggregate score of 74.18 and a judge-assigned result-behavior score of 5.04/10. These results show that strong semantic classification does not necessarily imply accurate prediction of detailed execution behavior, highlighting a gap in current LLM reasoning over compiler IRs. By exposing this gap through execution-validated program pairs, MLIRBench provides a reproducible foundation for studying semantic reasoning over compiler IRs and related tasks such as program repair and semantic classification.
entries.comment: Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027)

entries.title: Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types
entries.abstract: Distributed systems increasingly rely on randomisation; yet, verification techniques for such systems remain separate from the programming abstractions used to build them. This paper proposes the first probabilistic extension of general multiparty session types - typing sessions bottom-up, with no global specification - deriving quantitative properties of a multiparty session from its session types alone. Our types combine probabilistic choice with nondeterministic choice that abstracts data-dependent control, and allow separated choices, where each branch of a selection or branching may involve a different participant - a combination beyond previous probabilistic multiparty session type systems. To achieve this, we develop a novel probabilistic subtyping relation and merge operator, using which we prove type soundness and session fidelity. The semantics of typing contexts separates nondeterministic resolution, probabilistic choice, and synchronisation, so that every typing context induces a finite Markov decision process. On it, we derive sound lower bounds, holding under every fair adversarial scheduler, on the probability that a session is deadlock-free and live - the first behavioural property guarantees, partial or otherwise, for a probabilistic session calculus. To connect session types with probabilistic model checking, we introduce the first translation from session types into the PRISM modelling language, and prove it sound and complete with respect to our operational semantics. We implement the framework in the toolchain Prose, which translates probabilistic multiparty session typing contexts into PRISM and checks safety, deadlock-freedom, and liveness.
entries.comment: 108 pages, full version of "Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types" appearing at POPL 2027

entries.title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
entries.abstract: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

entries.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
entries.abstract: Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications. We take seven different portability frameworks—covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches—and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.

entries.title: CFGKAT: A Complete Calculus for Non-Local Control Flow
entries.abstract: CFGKAT is an extension of guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests (GKAT) that adds non-local control flow (e.g., break, goto) while maintaining an efficient decision procedure. An axiomatization of equivalence for CFGKAT presents unique barriers created by the presence of non-local control flow and contextual semantics of goto which compromises compositional reasoning. In this paper, we overcome these barriers and present a sound and complete axiomatization of program equivalence in CFGKAT. We verify the loop case of the Erosa-Hendren goto elimination algorithm, a difficult syntactic metatheorem which requires reasoning about fixpoints, control-flow contexts, and mutable state. We mechanize the metatheory and case study in Rocq.

entries.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
entries.abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

entries.title: Retargetable Compilation for Tensor Kernels via a Unified Layout Abstraction
entries.abstract: Modern hardware accelerators achieve high performance through specialized instructions coupled with tightly managed memory hierarchies. These instructions impose strict layout requirements on their operands: where tensor fragments reside, how they are organized, and how parallel units access them. Such instruction-visible layout is critical to kernel performance, as it determines whether instructions execute correctly and how much data movement they incur. However, existing compilers either scatter layout requirements across handwritten programs and local scheduling rules, or provide layout representations and conversions specific to a single class of targets. Both approaches expose the same abstraction gap: the absence of a unified model for instruction layout requirements across backends. This paper presents Arknife, a retargetable compiler that treats instruction-visible layout as first-class instruction semantics. Its central idea is a constraint-based layout algebra: tensor layouts map logical axes to hardware axes spanning parallel levels and memory spaces. Instruction operands declare layout requirements, and target-provided repairs resolve conflicts. Layouts are then solved globally across the program. ISA-specific layout facts are supplied by target-side instruction descriptions rather than hardcoded in the compiler. Retargeting reuses the layout algebra and solver while defining the new target's instructions and their operand requirements. We evaluate Arknife across x86 CPU, Hexagon NPU, and NVIDIA A100 GPU. Arknife matches cuBLAS on A100, and on x86 and Hexagon outperforms vendor-optimized libraries by 2.17× and 3.78× and the retargetable compiler MISAAL by 5.08× and 4.53×, respectively.

entries.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems in Grounded Arithmetic
entries.abstract: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic in which every term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation. RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it proves the hypothesis decided. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, how Gödel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA and for systems built on it. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so the implications the textbook proof of the second theorem uses fail while its entailments and rules hold: Gödel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence Con, and RGA derives its own second theorem as the entailment Con¬Pr(Con) and as one sentence quantified over proofs. The second theorem is then proved once, for every Gödel extension of RGA: an entailment relation on RGA's language, closed under RGA's rules, with a checker that meets three structural conditions, NEC, D3 and EXPL as proof transformers, D1 as closed acceptance, and consistency. D2 is not among the conditions. RGA with its checker is one instance. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA), RGA with ground induction, is another, its checker adding one rule detector, and IGA does not derive its consistency sentence for it. Adoption, a reflection rule whose premise is a derived warrant that the checker accepts computed proofs of every instance of a universal, gives consistent extensions RGA⁺ and IGA⁺. RGA⁺ derives RGA's consistency sentence and IGA⁺ derives RGA's and IGA's, so each strictly extends its base, and IGA⁺ both. The second theorem holds at every adopted notation claim, and adopting Turing's code for that claim's checker derives its consistency sentence, so no claim certifies itself. Whether IGA alone derives RGA's consistency sentence is open, and the paper names what two routes to an answer need.
entries.comment: 103 pages; splits the Goedel incompleteness material out of Internal Reasoning companion paper 2608.16140, which is getting a corresponding major update

entries.title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
entries.abstract: Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability, producing useful counterexamples in a single pass. Our key insight is to train counterexample generation not as a standalone validation task, but as a data-driven diagnostic objective: a counterexample is useful when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof and verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, repair rationale, and repaired proof in one trajectory, optimized with reinforcement learning from Verus feedback and a proof-code safety gate. To guide the order of invariant repairs, TopoVerus introduces a curriculum with a topological graph reward based on invariant dependencies derived from inductiveness tests, which encourages counterexample generation to follow the same topological order. Across seven Verus benchmarks with 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6%/72.2% weighted-average Safe-Pass@1/Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7/6.3 points. We also show that TopoVerus's learned counterexamples can directly augment the reasoning of existing LM-based proof repair approaches, improving their success rate by 64.3% compared to chain-of-thought diagnostics.

entries.title: Context Types: Bunched Modalities for Unifying Safety and Reachability
entries.abstract: Most type systems are designed to verify safety properties: the judgement e: τ holds if e may evaluate to any value contained in the denotation of τ, but nothing more. More recent type systems have considered the complementary class of reachability properties: in these systems, the typing judgment holds if e must be able to evaluate to every value denoted by τ, and possibly more. This paper introduces a refinement type system for higher-order functional programs where types can capture both safety and reachability properties. Simultaneously supporting both is challenging because each imposes different constraints on how variable bindings in a typing context are interpreted. We address this challenge by treating typing contexts as a kind of resource that mediates which capabilities are available when typing a program. We formalize this notion by developing a resource algebra of contextual capabilities and a bunched modal context logic over this algebra. We then interpret our type system in this logic, establishing soundness with respect to a denotational semantics that unifies safety and reachability guarantees within a single typing judgement.

entries.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
entries.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language 3 (OpenQASM 3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

entries.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
entries.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
entries.comment: 87 pages, 13 tables. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23988871 . The programs and their outputs are in the artifact, with a verifier that reruns every program and holds each reported number to the output line it rests on. Companion to arXiv:2608.03473, arXiv:2608.09761, arXiv:2609.10600, arXiv:2610.08854 and arXiv:2610.30168

entries.title: A Hoare Logic for Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
entries.abstract: Programming language researchers have developed a wide array of tools to reason about probabilistic programs, but it remains unclear how to apply these proof techniques to continuous-time stochastic processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a verification method for properties of continuous-time stochastic processes by reasoning about them as standard programs. To demonstrate our approach, we define a continuous semantics for a probabilistic imperative language pWhile^dt by taking the Kuratowski limit of the standard semantics, which collects limit points of the standard program semantics as the time-step approaches zero. Then, we present a Hoare-style logic that uses loop invariants and decreasing functions to verify properties of continuous programs. To establish soundness, we identify a broad class of assertions that are preserved from the standard semantics to the continuous semantics. To demonstrate our approach, we verify properties of ten continuous-time stochastic processes modeled in pWhile^dt, including variants of Brownian motion and a stochastic hybrid system.

entries.title: Beating Rytter's Bound: All-Pairs CFL Reachability in O(n³(loglogn)²/(logn)²) Time
entries.abstract: Context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition are fundamental problems in program analysis and language theory. Despite years of effort, the best algorithms for these problems run in time O(n³/logn) on a word RAM model; they are based on an observation of Rytter in 1985 for 2NPDA which was adapted for CFL reachability by Chaudhuri in 2008. No better algorithm has been designed since. We give the first improvement to Rytter's algorithm. For both all-pairs context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition, we show a deterministic algorithm running in O(n³(loglogn)²/(logn)²) time and O(n^(2+ε)) words of space for every fixed 0<ε<1 on a word RAM. Our improvement is based on a new data structure that reports set differences using batched maintenance of exact intersection counts, allowing saturation to skip regions that contain no new reachability information.

entries.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
entries.abstract: Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible. We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has m binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean ℓ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth d. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample. From one start state, law checks at O(m²logm/ε) samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold ε after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance 1/2. For the worst start distribution, take ε=m^(-β) with fixed 0<β≤1. For d≤cm with fixed c<1/2, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when ℓ=Ω(m), where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is (1/2+o(1))m. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at ε=1/(32m) and d≤m/16, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is Θ(mlog(m/d)/logm), by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in m if writes are counted.

entries.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
entries.abstract: We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes—Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill—with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound d for every odd d≥3 and checks in 214 s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.

entries.title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF
entries.abstract: Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.

entries.title: Symbolic Synthesis with Token-Level LLM Guidance
entries.abstract: We propose a synergistic combination of classical program synthesis techniques and contemporary large language models (LLMs) to solve the problem of recursive program synthesis from first-order logic specifications. Our approach leverages the strengths of both paradigms: we use LLMs as a source of statistical bias to guide the search for a correct program. At the same time we use techniques from classical synthesis to short-circuit on semantically incorrect prefixes and to avoid sampling semantically equivalent responses. The statistical bias is derived from the next-token distribution of an LLM, which is highly context-dependent. We operate with the understanding that (1) there is some class of synthesis instances that can be discharged by small models and symbolic tools, and (2) every other instance can be decomposed into these instances. Therefore, our intention is to expand the reach of small, open-weight LLMs and symbolic synthesis techniques, not to compete with proprietary frontier models on every possible instance. These are different tools for different jobs. In our experimental evaluation, we find that our method solves more benchmarks than either small LLMs or classical synthesis techniques alone. Our method solves 30/32 benchmarks using only a Qwen2.5 model with 32 billion parameters. Qwen2.5 solves 0 benchmarks on its own, and only solves a few additional benchmarks when combined with traditional constrained decoding techniques.

entries.title: Representing Tensors as Compositions for Efficient Computation on Sparse and Structured Data
entries.abstract: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from O(mn²), with m the number of binary operations between tensors and n the number of tensor types, to O(m + k²), with k the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.

entries.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
entries.abstract: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand. We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings. On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.

entries.title: SPMW: A Grid-Based Programming Model for Scalable Accelerator Design
entries.abstract: Modern accelerators specialize recurring computation and replicate it across regular hardware structures to achieve high performance. Sustaining this parallelism requires equally deliberate data delivery. Yet design tools often express these structures as sequential programs or flatten them into separate hardware modules and connections. This obscures shared patterns and leads to repeated compiler work. We introduce Single Program, Multiple Connected Work Units (SPMW), a grid-based programming model for scalable accelerator design that makes grid regularity a first-class abstraction. SPMW decouples local work-unit behavior from grid connectivity and data delivery. To our knowledge, SPMW is the first programming model to retain regularity throughout the compilation process, combining behavioral HLS with structural RTL generation for both fixed-function and domain-specific instruction-programmable accelerators. We implement SPMW with a Python frontend and an MLIR-based compiler that synthesizes each distinct kernel configuration once for reuse across independent hardware instances. Preserving regularity also enables parallel compilation and functional simulation to accelerate iterative design feedback. We use SPMW to generate a 32x32 systolic array that reduces GEMM latency and parallel kernel-to-RTL compilation time by 4.36x and 619x relative to AutoSA. Our FFT achieves up to 2.65x lower latency than HP-FFT. Our mini-TPU and our SPMW implementation of the FEATHER accelerator demonstrate complex composition and outperform their RTL baselines. Parallel functional simulation provides up to 18.4x speedup over Vitis HLS C simulation on the mini-TPU workloads. SPMW is also agent-friendly: given the same design specification, all five coding agents produce SPMW designs that satisfy the correctness and latency requirements, with 7.51x lower token usage than for SystemVerilog.
